It also covers tear-off and disposal costs if a covered failure occurs. To qualify, the project must include one GAF shingle plus one product from each of five accessory categories: Leak Barrier, Roof Deck Protection, Starter Strip Shingles, Attic Ventilation, and Hip and Ridge Cap Shingles. An uncredentialed roofer who installs GAF shingles without Master Elite status cannot register a Golden Pledge — the warranty simply is not available to them.

LayerLock works by passing nails through two shingle courses so the asphalt-to-asphalt bond cures into a single holding layer, rather than relying on adhesive strips alone.

faqs.question: How long does a metal roof actually last?
faqs.answer: Standing-seam metal roofs routinely last 40 to 70 years with no major intervention beyond periodic inspections. That lifespan outlasts two or three asphalt roof cycles on the same house. The key variable is fastener design: concealed-fastener standing seam eliminates the main failure mode (exposed gasketed screws that degrade in UV and thermal cycling), while exposed-fastener panels are less expensive upfront but require periodic re-fastening over their life.

faqs.question: What is the difference between standing-seam and exposed-fastener metal?
faqs.answer: Standing-seam panels interlock at raised seams and attach to the deck with hidden clips — no screw penetrates the weather surface. Rain, wind, and UV have no path to a fastener or gasket. Exposed-fastener panels use screws driven directly through the face of the panel; the neoprene gaskets under each screw head are the long-term vulnerability. Standing seam is the right choice for a primary residence. Exposed-fastener panels are appropriate for outbuildings, barns, and commercial utility structures where budget matters more than longevity.

faqs.question: When does metal roofing make economic sense over asphalt?
faqs.answer: Metal earns its premium when you plan to stay in the home long-term, when your current roof is in its second or third replacement cycle, or when local hail and wind exposure makes a one-time investment in a tougher material worth more than the price of repeated asphalt replacements. The installed cost of standing-seam steel runs $10 to $16 per square foot; architectural asphalt runs $4 to $6. On a 2,000-square-foot home that gap is real — but a metal roof that lasts 50 years against two or three asphalt replacements over the same period closes the gap considerably.

faqs.question: Will a metal roof make my house hotter in the summer?
faqs.answer: Color and finish do more work here than the base material. Light-colored and unpainted Galvalume finishes reflect a meaningful portion of solar radiation; darker painted panels absorb more heat, similar to dark asphalt. Energy-efficient metal roofs with light or reflective finishes can reduce attic heat gain compared to dark asphalt, particularly in North Carolina's long cooling season. If energy performance is a priority, specify a lighter panel color and confirm the coating qualifies for any applicable utility rebates in your area.

faqs.question: Does metal roofing make more noise in rain and hail?
faqs.answer: On a properly installed roof with solid decking below — which is the standard for residential standing-seam work — the sound difference between metal and asphalt is minimal. The deck, insulation, and ceiling assembly absorb most impact sound. Open-frame agricultural metal buildings with no decking are the source of the rain-on-a-tin-roof noise most people have in mind; that is a different installation context entirely.

faqs.question: Which membrane — TPO, EPDM, or PVC — is right for my building?
faqs.answer: The right answer depends on your building's use, climate exposure, and what is currently on the roof. In Raleigh's warm climate, TPO is our most common recommendation for offices and retail — its heat-welded seams eliminate the adhesive seam failures that cause most flat-roof leaks, and its white surface qualifies for ENERGY STAR cool-roof designation, which can meaningfully reduce cooling loads. EPDM is the better choice in colder climates and on low-complexity roofs where budget is the primary driver. PVC is the correct membrane for buildings with kitchen exhaust vents, grease traps, or chemical exposure — TPO and EPDM degrade on contact with animal fats and petroleum solvents. We will tell you which membrane the building actually needs, not the one with the widest margin.

faqs.question: What is an NDL warranty and why does it matter for a commercial building?
faqs.answer: NDL stands for No Dollar Limit. It means the manufacturer covers the full cost of any covered repair — materials and labor — with no cap, for the warranty's full term, adjusted for real-world repair costs rather than locked to an original price. A standard prorated warranty pays a declining fraction of repair costs each year; by year 15 it may cover less than half. An NDL warranty is documented on a building's balance sheet as a risk-reduction asset. It transfers with the property, which matters when you sell, refinance, or lease — a prospective buyer or lender sees a 20-year NDL with 14 years remaining as a concrete, quantifiable protection. NDL warranties require installation by a manufacturer-certified contractor; certification level matters because a contractor certified for a 12-year prorated warranty is not automatically eligible to issue a 20-year NDL on the same manufacturer's product.

faqs.question: What does a commercial roof maintenance plan actually include, and is it required?
faqs.answer: Most single-ply membrane manufacturers require at least one documented annual inspection by an authorized contractor to keep the warranty valid. The maintenance plan is the mechanism that preserves the coverage you paid for. A standard plan includes two full inspections per year — spring and fall — along with drain and gutter cleaning, debris removal, and a written inspection report that becomes part of your warranty documentation trail. If you ever need to file a warranty claim, the inspection record is what proves the membrane was maintained per manufacturer requirements. Without it, the manufacturer can deny the claim regardless of what caused the failure. We provide the documentation package, not just the visit.

faqs.question: How much disruption should we expect during a commercial re-roof?
faqs.answer: Most light-commercial flat roofs are replaced in 2 to 7 business days. Larger or more complex buildings can run 10 or more days. TPO and EPDM single-ply systems reduce active construction time compared to multi-layer built-up systems because the membrane goes down in large sheets rather than multiple applied layers. We schedule sequentially so no portion of your roof is left open overnight, and we can structure work in phases — completing one section before opening the next — when continuous operations require it. Night shifts and weekend installations are available for buildings where any daytime disruption is unacceptable. We discuss operating schedule constraints at the assessment stage, before scope is finalized.

faqs.question: How do we budget for a commercial roof replacement before we have a formal bid?
faqs.answer: Installed cost ranges by membrane type, based on current market data: TPO runs $5–$10 per square foot; EPDM runs $4–$9 per square foot; PVC runs $8–$15 per square foot; standing-seam steel runs $10–$16 per square foot. A 5,000 square foot flat roof — a common light-commercial footprint — typically falls in the $20,000–$75,000 range depending on membrane selection, insulation requirements, and whether tear-off is included. Tear-off adds $1–$3 per square foot. Labor accounts for 40–60% of total project cost, and that fraction rises on roofs with complex drainage, multiple penetrations, or difficult access. These are planning ranges, not quotes — deck condition, insulation R-value requirements, and local permit fees all affect the final number. A site assessment is the only way to produce a defensible budget figure.

faqs.question: How does TPO compare to EPDM for a commercial building in Raleigh?
faqs.answer: For warm-climate markets like Raleigh, TPO's heat-welded seams and solar reflectivity give it a real performance edge over EPDM. EPDM uses adhesive or tape seams — the industry's leading flat-roof leak cause — and black EPDM absorbs heat rather than reflecting it. White EPDM is available but not the default. Where EPDM earns its place is in cold-northern climates where rubber flexibility at sub-zero temperatures matters most. In Raleigh's climate, TPO is the stronger spec for most commercial applications. Installed cost is comparable: TPO runs $5–$10 per sq ft, EPDM $4–$9 per sq ft.

faqs.question: Why is TPO less suited than PVC for restaurants or food-processing buildings?
faqs.answer: TPO has moderate resistance to grease and petroleum-based chemicals, but it degrades under sustained direct exposure to animal fats, vegetable oils, and industrial solvents. PVC membrane is specifically formulated to resist those substances and is the correct spec for any building with kitchen exhaust discharging onto the roof surface or direct chemical exposure. We will tell you this before we quote — installing the wrong membrane to save a few dollars per square foot creates a warranty-voiding liability you should not accept.

faqs.question: What is an NDL warranty and why does it matter for a commercial property?
faqs.answer: NDL stands for No Dollar Limit. Standard roofing warranties cap the manufacturer's liability — as repair costs rise with inflation or scope, that cap erodes coverage. An NDL warranty carries no dollar ceiling on covered repair costs for the warranty term, typically 15, 20, or 30 years. For commercial property owners, remaining NDL coverage is a documented balance-sheet asset that influences purchase decisions, lease negotiations, and portfolio capital planning. It requires installation by a manufacturer-certified contractor and annual inspection documentation to stay valid — the maintenance program is the warranty-preservation mechanism, not an optional add-on.

faqs.question: What does the installation process actually disrupt for a business that stays open?
faqs.answer: Most commercial TPO replacements run two to seven business days. Tear-off is the noisiest phase, typically days one and two. We can phase the work to keep active sections of roof intact and move in sections around operating HVAC or rooftop equipment. We coordinate sequencing with your facilities or property manager before work begins — not the morning of. If your business has noise-sensitive hours or tenant lease requirements around construction, tell us during the assessment and we will build that into the schedule.

Labor accounts for 40–60 percent of that total. We do not quote per-square-foot numbers without a site inspection — roof complexity and substrate condition are the variables that move cost within that range, and a number given without seeing the building is a guess, not a quote.

faqs.question: How does EPDM compare to TPO — and when should I choose one over the other?
faqs.answer: The honest answer depends on your building and climate. EPDM rubber stays flexible in cold temperatures and has the longest documented track record on flat roofs — it has been the standard on residential additions and smaller commercial roofs for decades. TPO has heat-welded seams, which are a stronger bond than adhesive, and reflects more heat in summer (EPDM is typically black and absorbs heat). If your flat roof is on a sun-baked commercial building in a warm climate, TPO's reflectivity can matter. If it's on a residential addition or a building in a market where cold-weather flexibility is the priority, EPDM is hard to beat. We walk through both options with every flat-roof client before we write a proposal.

faqs.question: What do adhesive seams mean for long-term performance?
faqs.answer: Seam failure is the single leading cause of flat-roof leaks across all single-ply systems, and EPDM uses adhesive or tape rather than TPO's heat-welded bond. Done correctly — right adhesive, right temperature, proper dwell time — adhesive seams last the life of the membrane. Done incorrectly, they can begin to peel within five to ten years. This is why installation quality matters more on EPDM than almost any other roofing material. We will not apply adhesive seams outside the manufacturer's temperature window, and we schedule around weather rather than rush a job.

faqs.question: What does EPDM cost for a typical residential addition or small flat roof in Raleigh?

A small addition in the 300 to 600 square foot range is a straightforward job; a larger low-slope garage or commercial suite adds scope. We do not quote off square footage alone — an accurate number requires looking at the deck condition, drain locations, and penetration count. Call us for a free on-site assessment and written scope before you compare bids.

faqs.question: Is EPDM right for my home addition or low-slope roof section?
faqs.answer: EPDM is one of the most proven choices for residential additions, low-slope connector roofs between structures, flat garage roofs, and smaller commercial buildings where heat-welding equipment is impractical. It is not the right call if the roof has significant grease or chemical exhaust exposure — those applications call for PVC. It is also worth a conversation if your addition has generous sun exposure and cooling costs are a concern, because white TPO would reflect more heat. For a straightforward residential flat section with no special chemical or exhaust exposure, EPDM at a proper installation has a 25 to 30 year baseline service life and costs less than TPO.

faqs.question: How do I know when my EPDM roof needs to be replaced versus repaired?
faqs.answer: Most EPDM issues — open seams, cracked pipe boots, punctures from foot traffic — are repairable if caught early. Signs that indicate replacement rather than repair: membrane has become brittle and is shrinking or pulling away from flashings at multiple points, ponding water areas show widespread granular chalking, or the membrane has been patched repeatedly and the repair patches are themselves failing. A professional inspection will tell you clearly which category you are in. We are not interested in selling a replacement when a repair covers it — we will tell you straight.

faqs.question: What counts as a roof emergency — and what can wait until morning?
faqs.answer: A roof emergency is any breach that is actively letting water into your living space, or a structural situation where delay makes the damage significantly worse. Active leaking through ceilings or walls, a large section of missing shingles after a storm, visible daylight through your attic, collapsed flashing around a chimney or vent stack, or a tree limb that has punched through the deck — these are emergencies. A few lifted shingles with no current rain in the forecast, minor granule loss, or surface staining you noticed last weekend are real issues that deserve prompt attention, but they are not a same-night call. We will be honest with you about the difference — and we will not charge emergency rates for a job that can be safely scheduled during business hours.

faqs.question: What does emergency tarping actually do, and how long can a tarp stay on?
faqs.answer: A tarp is a holding action, not a repair. It stops an open roof breach from admitting additional water while we assess the full scope of damage and schedule proper repairs. A correctly installed tarp is weighted or mechanically fastened at the edges so it cannot shift or channel water inward — an improperly secured tarp can make water intrusion worse. Most tarps are designed for short-term protection: a few days to a few weeks. They are not a substitute for repairs, and leaving one on for months increases the risk of deck damage underneath from trapped moisture. We will tell you exactly how long your tarp buys you and schedule the repair inside that window.

faqs.question: Will my homeowner's insurance cover emergency repairs?
faqs.answer: Most standard NC homeowner's policies cover sudden and accidental storm damage — the tarp, the emergency response, and the subsequent repair work are typically filed under the same claim as the storm event. What the policy will not cover is damage caused by deferred maintenance or pre-existing deterioration. We document everything at first contact — photos, timestamps, written condition notes — so your insurer has the evidence they need. North Carolina policies generally require prompt notice of a claim, often within 30 to 60 days of the storm date. Filing after that window can jeopardize coverage entirely. We do not negotiate your claim or act as a public adjuster — we give you thorough documentation and attend the adjuster inspection to make sure nothing legitimate gets missed.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a hail damage claim in North Carolina?
faqs.answer: Most NC homeowners policies require prompt notice — often within 30 to 60 days of the storm date. The three-year statute of limitations to take legal action is not the same as your notice window. If you are unsure, pull out your declarations page and call your agent today. Waiting to see whether the damage gets worse is one of the most common reasons claims get denied.

faqs.question: My neighbor got a free roof — can you waive my deductible?
faqs.answer: No, and be wary of any contractor who offers that. Waiving or discounting a deductible is insurance fraud under NC law — a Class H felony that exposes both the contractor and the homeowner to criminal charges. Your deductible is your policy's responsibility. What we do instead: make sure the insurance scope covers every dollar of legitimate damage so the money you do spend is working for you.

faqs.question: The storm wasn't that bad. Do I really need an inspection?
faqs.answer: Yes. A 2025 peer-reviewed study confirmed that hailstones under one inch — storms that never make local news — can fracture shingle bonds internally and significantly accelerate aging. The damage is invisible from the ground and invisible in the attic, but it reduces your roof's resistance to the next storm. A documented inspection is the only way to know what you are dealing with.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an RCV and an ACV policy?
faqs.answer: Replacement Cost Value (RCV) pays what it costs to replace your roof today, minus your deductible. Actual Cash Value (ACV) pays that same number minus depreciation for the roof's age — on a 20-year-old roof, an ACV policy might generate a $3,000 check toward a $15,000 job. This distinction matters before you file. If you are unsure which policy you carry, check your declarations page under 'loss settlement' — we are glad to help you read it.

faqs.question: How is wind damage different from hail damage on a roof?
faqs.answer: Wind damage follows the prevailing storm direction — lifted tabs, creased shingles, and missing shingles cluster on the windward face of the roof and run in a consistent pattern. Hail damage is random: circular bruises and granule loss scattered across the entire deck with no directional signature. An adjuster and a trained roofing inspector look for that pattern first because it determines which coverage applies.

faqs.question: Can a few missing shingles really cause a serious leak?
faqs.answer: Yes — and faster than most homeowners expect. Each shingle is part of an overlapping waterproofing system. When even two or three are gone, the underlying roofing felt (underlayment) is exposed directly to rain. Felt is a secondary barrier, not a finished weather surface. Sustained rain, especially driven by wind, can saturate felt within hours and reach the wood decking beneath. Wet decking swells, warps, and begins to rot — what started as a small blow-off becomes a structural repair if it sits uncorrected for a single season.

faqs.question: What should I do immediately after wind damages my roof?
faqs.answer: First, document what you can safely see from the ground — photographs with timestamps are evidence your insurer will use. Do not climb the roof yourself in post-storm conditions. Call a licensed contractor for an emergency assessment and temporary tarping if sections are open to the sky. Then contact your insurance carrier promptly — most NC policies require notice within 30 to 60 days of the storm event. Waiting to "see if it gets worse" can cost you the ability to file.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an RCV and an ACV policy for wind damage?
faqs.answer: Replacement cost value (RCV) policies pay what it costs to replace damaged materials at today's prices, minus your deductible. Actual cash value (ACV) policies apply depreciation — a 15-year-old roof might be considered 60% through its useful life, meaning the payout is 40% of replacement cost before your deductible comes out. On a $14,000 job that could be a $2,800 check. Review your declarations page before a storm hits so there are no surprises when you need to file.

faqs.question: Are ridge caps and drip edge covered in a wind damage claim?
faqs.answer: Ridge caps and drip edge are among the first components to fail in high winds — ridge caps sit at the highest exposure point and drip edge is unsupported at the perimeter. Both are covered components under most homeowner policies when wind is the named cause of loss. A thorough inspection documents these specifically because adjusters can overlook edge and ridge in a quick walk-through. We photograph and itemize every damaged component so nothing legitimate is left out of the scope of loss.

faqs.question: Can you waive or cover my deductible?
faqs.answer: No — and any roofer who offers to is breaking the law. In North Carolina, waiving, absorbing, or discounting a homeowner's insurance deductible is insurance fraud under N.C.G.S. § 58-2-161, a Class H felony that applies to both the contractor and the homeowner. We do not offer it, and you should walk away from any company that does. What we do offer: thorough documentation to make sure the insurer's scope covers every dollar of legitimate damage, so your deductible is the only out-of-pocket cost you carry.

faqs.question: Can you handle my insurance claim for me?
faqs.answer: We can support your claim process with inspection documentation, an on-site presence at the adjuster meeting, and a supplement request if covered items were missed. What we cannot do — and will not do — is negotiate your settlement, represent you with your insurer, or act as a public adjuster. That requires a separate license under N.C.G.S. § 58-33A-10, and a contractor cannot hold both a roofing license and a public adjuster license simultaneously. The settlement stays between you and your carrier. We give you the documentation to stand on solid ground when you get there.

faqs.question: My roof looks fine from the ground. Do I still need an inspection after a storm?
faqs.answer: Yes. Hail damage is often invisible from the ground. A trained inspector looks for granule loss that exposes the black fiberglass mat, soft circular bruising in the asphalt layer, and dents on soft metals like gutters, downspouts, and chimney caps — all of which are adjuster-recognized evidence. A 2025 peer-reviewed study (Frontiers in Materials) confirmed that hailstones under one inch in diameter can significantly reduce a shingle's resistance to future weather and accelerate aging, even when the damage is not visible at street level. The inspection costs you nothing. Missing documented damage can cost you the claim.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a storm damage claim in North Carolina?
faqs.answer: Most NC homeowner policies require prompt notification — often within 30 to 60 days of the storm date. This is not the same as the three-year statute of limitations to sue your insurer; that is the deadline to pursue a legal dispute, not the deadline to notify your carrier. Waiting to 'see if it gets worse' can result in your insurer denying coverage for failure to report promptly. Call your insurer and call us as soon as you suspect storm damage.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an RCV and an ACV policy for a roof claim?
faqs.answer: Replacement Cost Value (RCV) policies pay for a new roof minus your deductible, regardless of how old your current roof is. Actual Cash Value (ACV) policies pay the depreciated value of your roof at the time of loss — on a 20-year-old roof, that could mean a check for roughly $3,000 toward a $15,000 job. Check your declarations page or call your agent before a storm, not after. If you have an ACV policy, we will give you an honest picture of what the payout is likely to cover and what the gap will be.

whatToExpect.heading: 5 Factors That Determine Your Actual Price
bullets: Roof footprint, not home square footage, is what you pay for — a single-story 2,000 sq ft home has nearly twice the roof area of a two-story home the same size, so story count is one of the first questions on every estimate.

Pitch and slope add 30–50% to labor costs on steep roofs (8/12 pitch and above) because the crew works slower, uses safety equipment, and carries higher workers' compensation exposure — that cost is real and shows up in every honest bid.

Every layer of old roofing that has to come off adds $0.40–$2.00 per square foot in tear-off and disposal fees, so a home that's been re-roofed over once or twice carries meaningfully higher base costs before a single new shingle is installed.

Rotted or damaged decking is the hidden-cost risk on every job — it can't be assessed until old shingles are stripped, so any contractor who quotes a firm price without a written allowance for decking repair is leaving you exposed to surprise charges at $2–$5 per square foot or $75–$120 per sheet.

Material choice is the single largest variable in the total project price — the gap between standard architectural asphalt and standing-seam metal on the same Raleigh home can exceed $20,000, so matching material to budget and use case is the most important conversation before a number is ever written down.

faqs.question: What does a roof replacement actually cost in Raleigh, NC?
faqs.answer: For a typical Raleigh home, installed costs run $10,500–$22,000 for standard architectural asphalt shingles. NC runs 15–20% below the national average, so Raleigh homeowners generally land below what you'll see quoted on national cost sites. The range is wide because roof footprint, pitch, layers to tear off, and material choice all move the number. A 1,700 sq ft home on a standard pitch with one layer to remove and GAF Timberline HDZ typically lands in the $9,500–$11,000 range. A steeper roof, a second layer to tear off, or a premium material pushes that number meaningfully higher. We quote after measuring — not before.

faqs.question: What's the difference between standard and premium shingles, and is the upgrade worth it?
faqs.answer: Standard architectural asphalt (GAF HDZ, Owens Corning Duration, CertainTeed Landmark) runs $4.11–$5.57 per square foot installed and carries a 25-year manufacturer-backed workmanship warranty on a Golden Pledge or Platinum Protection system. Designer and premium lines run $4.39–$5.95 installed and add features like Class 4 impact resistance, longer algae warranties, and heavier weight for a more dimensional appearance. The upgrade is most defensible if you're in a hail-prone area (Class 4 shingles can qualify for insurance premium reductions), if the home has a high-visibility roofline where curb appeal matters, or if you're planning to sell within five years and want a transferable manufacturer warranty as a selling point.

faqs.question: Will my insurance cover the replacement, and how does that work?
faqs.answer: For storm-damaged roofs, the average insurance payout for a hail or wind claim in NC runs $12,000–$17,000 — most homeowners pay only their deductible out of pocket on a replacement cost value (RCV) policy. The critical detail is policy type: an RCV policy pays the full cost to replace with like materials, minus your deductible. An actual cash value (ACV) policy depreciates the payout based on roof age — a 20-year-old roof on an ACV policy can result in a check as low as $3,000 toward a $15,000 job. We conduct a thorough post-storm inspection and provide written documentation with photos. We can meet your insurance adjuster on-site to ensure all covered damage is reviewed. We do not negotiate your claim or act as a public adjuster — the settlement stays between you and your insurer.

faqs.question: Can I finance a new roof, and what does that actually cost per month?
faqs.answer: Yes. A $12,000 roof replacement financed over 60 months at 8.99% APR is approximately $249 per month — less than most car payments, protecting the largest asset you own. Ask about promotional payment options when you request your quote. One disclosure worth knowing: some roofing financing programs advertise deferred-interest plans. These are not the same as 0% interest — interest accrues during the promotional period and is back-charged in full if the balance isn't paid before the promo window closes. We'll explain the terms of any financing option clearly before you sign anything. Financing is subject to credit approval.

faqs.question: How do I know if I need a full replacement or just a repair?
faqs.answer: A repair is often the right call for isolated damage — a few missing shingles after a wind event, a single flashing failure, or localized granule loss on an otherwise young roof. A replacement typically makes more economic sense when the roof is within 5 years of its expected lifespan, when damage covers more than 30% of the surface, or when a second layer of old shingles is already in place (a third layer is not permitted under NC building code and requires full tear-off). The honest answer can only come after an inspection — any contractor who recommends a full replacement from the driveway, without getting on the roof, is selling, not assessing.
